BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

Sport

By Marnie Vinall

Topic:AFL

Wed 1 Jul 2026 at 3:51pm

Wed 1 Jul 2026 at 4:11pm

Matthew Pavlich marches in this year's Mardi Gras for the Sydney Swans. (Supplied: Sydney Swans)

Ahead of the 2015 AFL season, Fremantle players were told about a new initiative over in NSW.

They were due to fly over for a preseason match against Sydney and before they left, were briefed about Pride work the Swans were starting to do.

They wanted to trial an AFL-sanctioned Pride game against the Dockers at Drummoyne Oval, with rainbow-decorated goal post pads, 50-metre arcs and goal umpire flags.

At the time, Fremantle legend Matthew Pavlich was not too excited about playing a preseason scrap all the way in Sydney, especially as he was in the twilight of his playing career.

"So, regrettably [I] jumped on a plane," he told ABC Sport.

But excitement started to take hold on the way over. The Pride initiative would give an atmosphere and occasion to a game that wouldn't necessarily be there in a standard preseason game.

Matthew Pavlich with Rainbow Swans chair Sarina Jackson. (Supplied: Sydney Swans)

"The crowd certainly showed up and brought it to life in what was a pretty carnival-like atmosphere," Pavlich said.

"I remember there were lots of pride flags and colour and atmosphere in the crowd and I also remember a young Isaac Heeney taking a few speccies and working out that this guy was going to be alright."

Pavlich cannot remember who won that day. He thinks it might have even been one of those games where six quarters were played instead of four.

But the game was deemed enough of a success that the following year, the first official Pride game for premiership points was held between Sydney and St Kilda in season.

Fast forward a decade and both clubs have hosted dedicated Pride games over the years and been at the forefront of LGBTQIA+ conversations in the league.

And Pavlich, who retired from the Dockers after a club record 353 games over 17 seasons, nine as captain, eventually found himself at the helm of Swans. He was announced as CEO in late 2025, taking over from Tom Harley.

Matthew Pavlich was announced as the CEO of the Sydney Swans in 2025. (Getty: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

At the Swans' Pride launch earlier in the week, he asked the crowd if anyone knew who Sydney first played a Pride game against. A fan in the crowd shot her hand straight up and confidently said "Fremantle".

While Pavlich asking the question was a bit of a clue, he said that moment also reflected the deep passion the Swans' Pride community had in the history of the club and the LGBTQIA+ work it did. It was something he learnt quickly about.

Sydney Swans supporters turn out for Pride games. (Getty: Kelly Defina)

"This [Pride initiatives] is about showing up to the community well and doing things the right way and for the right reasons, and clearly this resonates very strongly for our Sydney fans," said Pavlich, who marched with the Swans' cohort in this year's Mardi Gras.

"What I've learned is that this history goes well beyond 2015, it goes all the way back to the '80s, when the club first moved up here from South Melbourne, and was well established here in the eastern suburbs of Sydney, and Oxford Street, and Paddington, and then that community that's been well embraced by our club."

The Sydney Swans take part in the Sydney Gay & Lesbian Mardi Gras Parade in 2024. (Getty: Jenny Evans)

Not even a year in as the new boss of the Swans, he found himself having tough conversations about Pride.

Sydney was originally scheduled to play St Kilda in its Pride game this year but made the switch to the Western Bulldogs at the SCG amid the fallout from the Lance Collard homophobic slur case.

St Kilda's Collard was embroiled in a complex tribunal case for using a homophobic slur in a VFL match. He had his sanction controversially reduced from nine weeks to four, with two weeks suspended, by the league's appeals board.

The club fully supported him throughout the hearings.

The Swans' Pride guernsey is seen during a 2021 match against St Kilda.  (Getty: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

Given the high-profile nature of the case, the Rainbow Swans, the official LGBTQIA+ supporter group of the club, believed playing the Pride game against St Kilda would have been a distraction from the joy and celebration the event was supposed to embody.

"We spoke to the AFL about it and a number of other people in the community about what's the right thing to do here to celebrate it properly and how do we see and listen and make sure that the Pride community belong in the match," he said.

"Importantly, [it was] a large section of the Pride community that we wanted to listen to and make sure that the game was appropriately celebrated, which it will be.

"We knew it was going to be challenging conversations and we knew it was going to be some tough decisions but at the same time, you balance all these things up about what's the right thing to do and how do we positively keep celebrating the Pride community? And on balance, that was the decision that was made."
